title: Speech and conversation
note: Sort talk words by what they describe: how much someone says (loquacious, taciturn, terse, prolix), how it sounds (orotund, stentorian, mellifluous), and what the speaker is after (exhort, importune, cajole). Latin loqui, to speak, sits inside loquacious, circumlocution and elocution.

items.a: tending to talk a great deal
d: brief to the point of rudeness
pleasantly smooth and sweet in sound
items.ex: Our loquacious guide narrated every mile of the drive, including the parking lot.

items.a: habitually saying very little
items.ex: The taciturn farmer answered a ten-minute question with a single nod.

items.a: speaking fluently, readily, and at length
d: speaking in a booming, very loud voice
unwilling to say anything at all
items.ex: Shy in class, she turned voluble the moment the talk turned to baseball.

items.a: brief to the point of curtness
items.ex: His terse email read, in full: "No. See me."

items.a: brief and full of meaning
items.ex: Her pithy summary did more work than the forty-page report.

items.a: tediously long and wordy
items.ex: The prolix contract took three pages to say "pay on time."

items.a: pompous and inflated in language
items.ex: The candidate's bombastic promises outran any plan to keep them.

items.a: fluent but shallow or insincere
items.ex: He had a glib answer for every question and a real answer for none.

items.a: a roundabout way of saying something
d: a short saying that states a truth
items.ex: Through careful circumlocution, the memo never quite used the word "layoffs."

items.a: a person taking part in a conversation
d: a person who scolds at length
a person who refuses to speak
items.ex: The professor treated each student as a serious interlocutor, not an audience.

items.a: quick, witty replies in conversation
items.ex: The dinner sparkled with repartee until someone brought up politics.

items.a: good-humored teasing
items.ex: The team's raillery about his orange shoes never turned cruel.

items.a: a long, forceful, often scolding speech
items.ex: The coach's halftime harangue could be heard in the parking lot.

items.a: a bitter, sustained verbal attack
items.ex: His review was less a critique than a diatribe against the whole genre.

items.a: insulting, abusive language
items.ex: The debate dissolved into invective, and the moderator gave up.

items.a: to speak in a loud, dramatic, rhetorical way
d: to take back an earlier statement
items.ex: He stood on a chair to declaim the poem to the whole café.

items.a: full and resonant in sound, of a voice
items.ex: The actor's orotund voice filled the hall without a microphone.

items.a: to protest or denounce loudly and bitterly
d: to speak in a soft, soothing way
items.ex: Columnists fulminated for weeks about the new parking fees.

items.a: to pester with persistent requests
d: to praise in a formal speech
to explain a point in detail
items.ex: Vendors importuned every tourist who stepped off the ferry.

items.a: to coax with flattery or gentle persuasion
items.ex: She cajoled her brother into driving by promising to buy lunch.

items.a: to urge earnestly to do something
items.ex: The captain exhorted the crew to hold on for one more hour.

items.a: to raise an objection or show reluctance
items.ex: Asked to chair the committee, she demurred, citing her workload.

items.a: to state firmly that something is true
d: to avoid giving a clear answer
items.ex: The witness averred that the gate had been locked at nine.

items.a: to explain in careful detail
d: to summarize in a few words
items.ex: Ask him about tides and he will expound for an hour.

items.a: to make clear; to throw light on
items.ex: One diagram elucidated what three paragraphs had muddled.

items.a: sweet and smooth to hear
items.ex: The narrator's mellifluous voice made even the tax guide soothing.

items.a: extremely loud and powerful, of a voice
items.ex: A stentorian "Quiet!" from the back silenced the room.

items.a: loudly and insistently outspoken
items.ex: The plan drew vociferous opposition from the neighbors.

items.a: in a quiet voice, so as not to be overheard
items.ex: "He's wrong," she said sotto voce, while the speaker went on.

items.a: the art of clear, expressive speaking
d: the art of the witty reply
items.ex: Years of elocution lessons gave her vowels a radio polish.
